section.title: Instructions for the Priests
section.sectionRationale: Having given the offerings from the worshiper's side, the LORD now turns to the priests themselves, the torah, the law or instruction, for how they are to handle the burnt, grain, and sin offerings, including the perpetual fire and the eating of most holy portions.
section.thesis: God gives Aaron and his sons detailed instructions for maintaining the altar's continual fire and for handling the burnt, grain, and sin offerings, teaching that the priests who mediate atonement must themselves treat every holy thing with exacting care.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the law of the burnt offering and its perpetual fire; the law of the grain offering, eaten by the priests in a holy place; and the law of the sin offering, most holy, requiring careful handling of its blood.

units.label: The perpetual fire
units.note: the law of the burnt offering

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,

“Command Aaron and his sons that this is the {{torah|law}} of the burnt offering: The burnt offering is to remain on the hearth of the altar all night, until morning, and the {{tamid|fire must be kept burning}} on the altar.
And the priest shall put on his linen robe and linen undergarments, and he shall remove from the altar the ashes of the burnt offering that the fire has consumed and place them beside it.
Then he must take off his garments, put on other clothes, and carry the ashes outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place.

The fire on the altar shall be kept burning; it must not be extinguished. Every morning the priest is to add wood to the fire, arrange the burnt offering on it, and burn the fat portions of the peace offerings on it.
The fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it must not be extinguished.

units.label: The law of the grain offering
units.note: eaten in a holy place, most holy

verses.text: Now this is the law of the grain offering: Aaron's sons shall present it before the LORD in front of the altar.
The priest is to remove a handful of fine flour and olive oil, together with all the frankincense from the grain offering, and burn the memorial portion on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder. It must be eaten without leaven in a holy place; they are to eat it in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.
It must not be baked with leaven; I have assigned it as their portion of My offerings made by fire. It is {{qodeshQodashim|most holy}}, like the sin offering and the guilt offering.
Any male among the sons of Aaron may eat it. This is a permanent portion from the offerings made by fire to the LORD for the generations to come. Anything that touches them will become holy.”
Then the LORD said to Moses,

“This is the offering that Aaron and his sons must present to the LORD on the day he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening.
It shall be prepared with oil on a griddle; you are to bring it well-kneaded and present it as a grain offering broken in pieces, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
The priest, who is one of Aaron's sons and will be anointed to take his place, is to prepare it. As a permanent portion for the LORD, it must be burned completely.
Every grain offering for a priest shall be burned completely; it is not to be eaten.”

units.label: The law of the sin offering

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell Aaron and his sons that this is the law of the sin offering: In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the sin offering shall be slaughtered before the LORD; it is most holy.
The priest who offers it shall eat it; it must be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.
Anything that touches its flesh will become holy, and if any of the blood is spattered on a garment, you must wash it in a holy place.
The clay pot in which the sin offering is boiled must be broken; if it is boiled in a bronze pot, the pot must be scoured and rinsed with water.
Any male among the priests may eat it; it is most holy.
But no sin offering may be eaten if its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it must be burned.

torah.gloss: Law or instruction, from a root meaning to teach or point the way. Each offering in this chapter has its own torah, its own detailed instruction, showing that God's law is fundamentally a patient teaching of how to live and worship rightly, not a bare list of rules.

tamid.gloss: Continually, perpetually, without ceasing. The altar fire that must never go out, tamid, pictures unceasing access to atonement and worship, a fire that must be tended faithfully by the priests day and night.

qodeshQodashim.gloss: Most holy, the highest level of consecration. The grain and sin offerings eaten by the priests are qodesh qodashim, so holy that anything touching them becomes holy too, requiring careful handling and eating only in a sacred place.

basic.context: Having given instructions for worshipers bringing offerings, God now turns to the priests themselves, giving them the torah, the detailed instruction, for handling the burnt, grain, and sin offerings. The altar fire must never go out, the grain offering is eaten by the priests in a holy place, and the sin offering, most holy, requires such careful handling that even the pot it is cooked in must be broken or scoured.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes actual procedural instructions for Israel's old covenant priesthood, not a pattern for how Christian ministers today must handle sacred objects. Its abiding truth is that those who mediate access to God bear a serious responsibility to treat what is holy with exacting, careful reverence.
basic.originalLanguages: Each offering has its own torah, instruction, from a root meaning to teach, showing that law in Scripture is fundamentally patient guidance, not arbitrary restriction. The altar fire burns tamid, continually, and the priests' portions of the grain and sin offerings are qodesh qodashim, most holy, so sacred that contact with them makes ordinary things holy too.
basic.typology: The fire that must never go out pictures the unceasing, always available access to atonement that God provided for Israel, anticipating the permanently open access believers now have through Christ's finished work. The priests eating what is most holy, bearing the weight of the people's guilt as they consume the sin offering, foreshadows Christ, who bore the sin of His people in His own body.
basic.christ: Just as the priests bore away the guilt of the people by eating the sin offering, so Christ, our great High Priest, bore our sins in His own body on the tree, 1 Peter 2:24. The unceasing fire on the altar anticipates the once for all, never repeated sacrifice of Christ, whose atonement never needs to be relit or renewed.
basic.god: God cares intensely about the details of how His holy things are handled, not because He is arbitrary, but because holiness itself is contagious in this system, spreading to whatever touches it, and profaned by carelessness. He is a God who takes the mediating work of His priests with the utmost seriousness.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 2:24 says Christ bore our sins in His own body on the tree, echoing the priest who bore the sin offering by eating it. Hebrews 10:11-14 contrasts the priests who stood daily, offering repeated sacrifices, with Christ, who sat down after one sacrifice for sins forever. Hebrews 7:27 says Christ has no need to offer sacrifices daily as those priests did.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows God instructing His priests to treat every holy thing with exacting care, since holiness is not casual and guilt is not lightly handled. It anticipates Christ, our great High Priest, who bore our sin fully in His own body, and whose single sacrifice means the fire of atonement, once lit at the cross, never needs to be relit again.

context.literary:
Leviticus 6:8 begins a new block that runs to 7:38, and its opening verb signals the change. Chapters 1 to 5 were addressed through Moses to the whole people, 'Speak to the Israelites,' Leviticus 1:2 and 4:2. Here the word is 'Command Aaron and his sons,' 6:9. The same offerings are now described from the priests' side of the altar: what they must keep burning, what they may eat, where and how.

The block is organised by a repeated heading, 'this is the law of,' at 6:9, 6:14 and 6:25, continuing at 7:1 and 7:11, and gathered up in the summary of 7:37. Within this study the pattern gives three sections: the burnt offering, 6:8-13; the grain offering, 6:14-18, with an inserted rule for the high priest's own grain offering, 6:19-23, marked by its own speech formula; and the sin offering, 6:24-30.

The order differs from chapters 1 to 5. There the peace offering came third; here it is held back to 7:11, after the guilt offering. The likely reason is that this block moves from the most holy offerings, which only priests may touch or eat, to the peace offering, which ordinary worshipers share. The arrangement follows degrees of holiness rather than the worshiper's point of view.

The burnt offering section is framed by the fire. Verse 9 says 'the fire must be kept burning on the altar'; verses 12 and 13 say it twice more, the second time with 'continually' and 'it must not be extinguished.' Between the statements sits the ash removal, verses 10 and 11. The repetition makes the fire the centre of the priest's daily life.

Each of the eating rules turns on the same phrase, 'it is most holy,' 6:17, 6:25 and 6:29, and two sections end with a warning about contact, 'Anything that touches them will become holy,' 6:18 and 6:27. The chapter closes with an exception, 6:30, which ties back to the bulls of Leviticus 4 whose blood was carried inside.
context.historical:
The priests of Israel owned no tribal land. 'I am your portion and your inheritance,' God told Aaron, Numbers 18:20. The portions described here, the remainder of the grain offering and the meat of the sin offering, were a large part of how they lived. Eating them was both a stipend and a sacred duty.

The burnt offering altar stood in the open courtyard in front of the tent, and the morning and evening lambs of Exodus 29:38-42 burned on it every day. Keeping the fire alive through the night meant constant attention to wood and ashes. Long after Sinai, the returned exiles cast lots for 'the donation of wood' so that it could 'burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law,' Nehemiah 10:34. This chapter is the law they had in mind.

The priest's clothing reflects a sharp sense of sacred space. For work at the altar he wore linen, the material of his holy garments, Exodus 28:42 and Leviticus 16:4. To carry the ashes out of the camp he changed. Ezekiel later explains the logic: priests leaving the inner court are to change 'so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments,' Ezekiel 44:19. Linen was also cool; Ezekiel adds that they must not wear anything 'that makes them perspire,' Ezekiel 44:18.

The rule about pots reflects ordinary kitchen life. Clay vessels were cheap, porous and easily replaced; bronze was costly and hard. Blood spattered on a garment had to be washed in the holy place itself, 6:27, so that nothing most holy would be carried into common use.

The high priest's daily grain offering, 6:20, was offered in halves morning and evening. Later Israel kept this duty as part of the temple service; 1 Chronicles 9:31 records a Levite 'entrusted with baking the bread.'
context.canonical:
The fire of 6:12-13 has a history within Leviticus. When the tabernacle service began, 'fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering,' Leviticus 9:24. Many readers see the perpetual fire as the careful keeping of that divine flame, which is why the very next scene is so grave: Nadab and Abihu 'offered unauthorized fire,' Leviticus 10:1, and were consumed. The same fire fell again at the dedication of Solomon's temple, 2 Chronicles 7:1.

Leviticus 10:16-18 applies 6:26 and 6:30. Moses rebukes Eleazar and Ithamar for burning a sin offering whose blood had not gone inside; it should have been eaten, 'to take away the guilt of the congregation.' The rule about contagious holiness is taken up by Haggai, who asks the priests whether holy meat carried in a garment makes other food holy. They answer no, but defilement does spread, Haggai 2:11-14. Isaiah's commissioning comes by a coal 'from the altar' that touches his lips, and his sin is 'atoned for,' Isaiah 6:6-7. Malachi longs for someone to shut the temple doors so that priests will stop kindling 'useless fires on My altar,' Malachi 1:10.

The New Testament draws directly on these rules. Hebrews 13:10-11 says, 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat,' and explains why from 6:30 and Leviticus 16:27: the sin offerings whose blood entered the Holy Place were not eaten but burned outside the camp. Christ is that kind of offering. Hebrews 10:11-14 contrasts priests who stand 'day after day' with the one Priest who sat down. Revelation pictures a heavenly altar with fire and the prayers of the saints, Revelation 8:3-5, and Peter calls the church 'a holy priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel's priests to understand that their work was never finished. The people brought offerings when they chose or when they sinned, but the priest kept the fire every night and every morning. The altar's life depended on faithful, unglamorous routine: wood, ashes, clothing, the same tasks repeated for generations.

He also wanted them to learn that the holiness they handled was dangerous as well as precious. They could eat what was most holy, but only in the holy place, only if they were male descendants of Aaron, only in the prescribed way. What touched these offerings was affected by them. A careless priest could spread holiness where it did not belong, or treat it as common food.

And he wanted them to grasp that the priest was himself a worshiper, not above the system. He had his own grain offering, which he could not eat, 6:23, and a sin offering for himself would be burned, 6:30. The mediator stood under the same holiness he served. Israel's priests were to receive their living from the altar without ever forgetting that the altar was the LORD's.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These are commands to Aaron's house for the Sinai covenant, and they are not binding on the church. There is no Christian altar fire to tend, no holy courtyard, no sin offering to eat, because Christ's sacrifice was offered once and needs no maintenance, Hebrews 10:12-14. The New Testament does not transfer the Aaronic priesthood to church ministers; it describes the whole church as a priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9.

What carries over is the character the chapter builds. Faithful, daily attention to what God has entrusted is still a virtue; Paul's 'Pray without ceasing,' 1 Thessalonians 5:17, has the rhythm of the fire that must not go out. Reverence for holy things still matters, and Hebrews urges worship 'with reverence and awe,' because 'our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:28-29. The support of those who serve is still right, 1 Corinthians 9:13-14. The chapter's details belong to Israel; its seriousness belongs to every age.

debates.question: Why must a clay pot used to boil the sin offering be broken, while a bronze pot need only be scoured, verse 28?

views.label: Porous versus non porous materials
views.case: Clay is porous and can absorb residue from the most holy offering in a way that cannot be fully cleaned, so it must be destroyed, while bronze, being non porous, can be adequately scoured and reused. Leviticus 11:33 applies the same rule to clay vessels made unclean.

views.label: A picture of holiness that cannot be casually reused
views.case: Others see the broken pot as a vivid, tangible lesson that contact with what is most holy permanently changes an object, a symbol reinforcing the seriousness of handling sacred things even beyond a merely practical concern.

debates.bearing: Either reading underscores the same point, that the most holy offerings required a level of care matched to their sacredness, whatever the practical or symbolic reason for the specific rule.

debates.question: What does it mean that 'anything that touches them will become holy,' verses 18 and 27?

views.label: Holiness is contagious to objects
views.case: The plain sense is that the most holy offerings transmit holiness to whatever touches them, such as a garment or a vessel, which then belongs to the sanctuary and cannot return to ordinary use. That explains the washing in a holy place and the breaking of the clay pot, verses 27 and 28, and matches Exodus 29:37 and 30:29.

views.label: Only the holy may touch them
views.case: Some translate 'whoever touches them must be holy,' making the phrase a restriction on persons: only consecrated priests may handle these offerings. Verse 18 does begin 'Any male among the sons of Aaron may eat it,' which fits a rule about who is allowed.

views.label: Limited contagion
views.case: Haggai 2:12 shows priests ruling that holiness does not pass on by second hand contact, while uncleanness does, Haggai 2:13. On this view the contagion is real but direct and limited, a hedge around the sanctuary rather than a force that spreads outward.

debates.bearing: The first and third views fit together best: holiness does pass by direct contact, but it is not self-spreading the way impurity is. That asymmetry sets up the wonder of the Gospels, where Jesus touches the unclean and they become clean, Mark 1:41-42.

debates.question: When the priest eats the sin offering, 6:26, is he bearing the people's guilt or simply receiving his portion?

views.label: Eating is part of the atonement
views.case: Leviticus 10:17 says the sin offering 'was given to you to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them.' On this reading the priests' eating completes the rite; the holy priest absorbs and disposes of what the offering carried.

views.label: Eating is the priest's provision
views.case: Others read Leviticus 10:17 as describing the whole priestly ministry, not the eating alone, and note that 6:29 and 7:7 treat the meat as the priest's portion. The eating is his rightful share for mediating, as with the grain offering.

debates.bearing: The texts allow both, and the priest's portion was never merely a meal. Leviticus 10:17 at least makes the eating part of the priest's service in taking guilt away, which is why it had to be done in a holy place and why a sin offering for the priest himself could not be eaten.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening verb is tsav, 'command,' in 6:9, where chapters 1 to 5 had 'speak.' The shift is small but deliberate. The worshiper was told what he might bring; the priest is ordered what he must do. Jewish tradition names this portion of Leviticus after the word.

The fire language turns on two verbs. Yaqad, to burn, gives both the noun for the altar's 'hearth,' 6:9, and the repeated 'kept burning,' 6:9, 12 and 13. Kabah, to go out or be quenched, stands behind 'it must not be extinguished,' 6:12 and 13. The same verb is used of the temple lamp at Shiloh, 'before the lamp of God had gone out,' 1 Samuel 3:3, and of the Servant who treats the weak gently: 'a smoldering wick He will not extinguish,' Isaiah 42:3, applied to Jesus in Matthew 12:20. The fire God commands His priests to keep alive, His Servant keeps alive in the faintest believer.

The 'memorial portion' of 6:15 is azkarah, from zakar, to remember. The handful burned on the altar stands for the whole offering and brings the worshiper to God's remembrance. The angel's word to Cornelius, 'Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God,' Acts 10:4, uses this sacrificial idea for a Gentile's prayer.

'The priest who offers it shall eat it,' 6:26, is more vivid in Hebrew. The participle comes from the intensive stem of chata, the verb that in this stem means to purify or take away sin. The officiating priest is literally 'the one who de-sins it,' the one whose work removes the sin the offering carries. The phrase ties this chapter tightly to the purification language of Leviticus 4.

The high priest's grain offering is 'burned completely,' 6:22 and 23, from kalil, 'whole' or 'entire.' The same word appears alongside the burnt offering in Moses' blessing on Levi, 'whole burnt offerings on Your altar,' Deuteronomy 33:10, in Samuel's 'whole burnt offering,' 1 Samuel 7:9, and in David's 'whole burnt offerings,' Psalm 51:19. The point is that nothing is held back; the priest's gift goes entirely to God.

Finally, the verb in 'will become holy,' 6:18 and 27, is the simple stem of qadash. Its subject, 'anything that touches,' can be read as a thing or a person, which is why translations differ between 'will become holy' and 'must be holy.' The same phrase appears for the altar in Exodus 29:37 and the tabernacle furnishings in Exodus 30:29.

typology.type: The fire that must never go out, Leviticus 6:12-13
typology.fulfillment: The perpetual fire meant the altar was always ready: at any hour an Israelite could come, and the means of acceptance was burning. In Christ the readiness is personal and permanent. 'He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25, so that access to God never lapses. The escalation is that the altar fire needed daily fuel and priestly tending, while Christ's intercession rests on a sacrifice offered 'once for all,' Hebrews 7:27. The type falls short because a careless priest could let the fire die; nothing can interrupt the priesthood of the one who 'has been made perfect forever,' Hebrews 7:28.

typology.type: The priest eating the sin offering in the holy place, Leviticus 6:26
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus 10:17 says the sin offering was given to the priests 'to take away the guilt of the congregation.' The holy priest took into himself what carried the people's sin, within the sanctuary where it could do no harm. Christ does more than eat the offering: He is the offering and the priest together. 'He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The type falls short in that the Aaronic priest bore sin symbolically and could himself be a sinner; Christ bore it truly, being 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26.

typology.type: The high priest's grain offering, wholly burned, Leviticus 6:19-23
typology.fulfillment: From the day of his anointing the high priest offered a grain offering morning and evening that he could never eat. The mediator gave himself to God entirely and took nothing back. Christ's whole life was such an offering. 'For them I sanctify Myself,' John 17:19, and He 'gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. The type falls short because Aaron's offering was flour, a token of the man; Christ offered His own body, and the offering did not need repeating twice a day.

typology.type: Holiness that passes by touch, Leviticus 6:18 and 6:27
typology.fulfillment: In Leviticus the most holy offerings made what touched them holy, but Haggai 2:12-13 records that holiness did not spread the way defilement did. In the Gospels the pattern is reversed. Jesus touches a man with leprosy and says, 'Be clean!' Mark 1:41, touches the coffin of a dead son, Luke 7:14, and a bleeding woman is healed by touching His garments, Mark 5:27-30. In Him holiness finally proves stronger than uncleanness. The type falls short because the altar's holiness only sanctified objects; Christ's holiness heals people.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first through the contrast between standing and sitting. Its priests are never done. The fire must be fed every morning, the ashes removed, the grain offering made at dawn and dusk. Hebrews reads this unending routine as a confession: 'Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.' Then comes the turn: 'But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God,' Hebrews 10:11-12. What Aaron's sons could only maintain, Christ has completed.

It leads to Christ through the rule of 6:30. A sin offering whose blood entered the Holy Place could not be eaten; it had to be burned outside the camp. Hebrews 13:10-12 builds on exactly this: 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat,' because Christ's offering is the kind whose blood went into the sanctuary, and so 'Jesus also suffered outside the city gate.' The rule that kept priests from eating the highest sin offering becomes the proof that the old priesthood has no share in the new altar, while believers do.

It leads to Christ through the priest who bears sin. The priest's eating of the sin offering was linked to taking away guilt, Leviticus 10:17. Christ, the true priest, 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. He does not stand at a distance from the sin He removes.

It leads to Christ through holiness that touches. The altar's holiness passed by contact to garments and vessels. In Jesus, holiness passes to people: lepers, the dead, a woman who touches His cloak. He is the Holy One whose touch cleanses rather than being defiled.

And it leads to Christ through the fire itself. The altar fire was a gift from the presence of the LORD, Leviticus 9:24, to be kept, never replaced. At Pentecost the Spirit came with 'tongues like flames of fire,' Acts 2:3, on a new priesthood. The fire of God now rests on a people rather than an altar, because the sacrifice that altar pointed to has been made.

These links must be held with restraint. The ashes, the linen and the bronze pot are not coded prophecies of Christ. The connections rest on how Hebrews and the Gospels read the priesthood and its rules, and on the pattern the chapter itself establishes: a continual ministry, a holiness that marks what it touches, and a priest who bears the people's sin.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the one who never withdraws His welcome. The command that the fire be kept burning 'continually' is not about God's need but about Israel's access. Day and night the altar was ready. God's readiness to receive His people does not sleep, as the psalmist says, 'the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep,' Psalm 121:4.

It shows God's holiness as active and powerful. Holiness in Leviticus is not merely a moral quality but a reality that marks what it touches, 6:18 and 27. The God who dwells in the tent is so holy that even the pot that holds His offering is affected. That is why the priest must change clothes before going out among the people, 6:11. Holiness is a kind of weight or force, the presence of God pressing into the world.

It shows God as the provider for those who serve Him. Aaron's sons had no land, but God gave them 'a permanent portion from the offerings made by fire,' 6:18. He does not ask His servants to work for nothing. The same care stands behind Paul's argument that 'those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings,' 1 Corinthians 9:13.

It shows God as impartial even toward His own priests. The high priest's grain offering is burned completely, 6:23, and a sin offering for the priest may not be eaten, 6:30. God does not let His mediators profit from their own atonement. They stand before Him as worshipers who need grace like everyone else.

It shows God as a consuming fire who is also a giving fire. The same fire that consumed Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus 10:2, burned every day for Israel's acceptance. Hebrews joins both truths: 'let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. For our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:28-29.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to a steady devotion rather than occasional bursts. The fire was kept by daily wood and daily ashes, by people whose names are mostly lost. Faithfulness in ordinary service, offered to a holy God through the finished work of Christ, is itself a form of worship that He sees and values.

crossReferences.note: At the first service of the tabernacle, 'fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering.' Leviticus 6:12-13 commands that the altar fire never go out, and read together the two passages suggest the priests were keeping a flame God Himself had kindled, not one they had made.

Nadab and Abihu offer 'unauthorized fire' and die. The episode shows what is at stake in the fire rules of Leviticus 6: the priests must use only the fire God gave and follow only the way He commanded, because 'to those who come near Me I will show My holiness.'

Moses applies the rules of Leviticus 6:26 and 6:30. A sin offering whose blood did not go inside should have been eaten by the priests in the holy place, because it was given 'to take away the guilt of the congregation.' It is the clearest statement of what the priests' eating meant.

The returned exiles cast lots for supplying wood 'to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.' Centuries after Sinai, the command that the altar fire be kept burning shapes the life of a restored community, which organises itself so that the flame never fails.

Haggai asks the priests for a ruling: does holy meat carried in a garment make other food holy? No. Does contact with a corpse defile? Yes. The prophet uses the contagion rules of Leviticus 6:27 to show that the people's worship was being defiled by their condition, and that holiness does not spread as easily as impurity.

Ezekiel's priests wear linen in the inner court and change before going out to the people 'so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments.' It explains the change of clothes in Leviticus 6:10-11: holy garments belong to holy space.

A seraph takes a coal from the altar and touches Isaiah's lips: 'your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.' The altar fire of Leviticus 6 is here the means of cleansing a sinner directly, showing the fire as an instrument of grace and not only judgment.

'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.' Hebrews argues from the rule of Leviticus 6:30, that sin offerings whose blood entered the Holy Place were burned, not eaten. Christ is that offering, suffering outside the gate, so the new altar belongs to His people, not to the old priesthood.

The priests stand 'day after day' offering the same sacrifices, which never take away sins; Christ offered one sacrifice and 'sat down.' The daily fire and repeated offerings of Leviticus 6 are the background, and the contrast between standing and sitting carries the whole argument.

Christ 'always lives to intercede,' is 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' and does not need 'to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins.' Hebrews answers the two limits of Leviticus 6: the need for continual tending, 6:12-13, and the high priest's need of an offering for himself, 6:20-23.

Jesus touches a man with leprosy and he is cleansed. In Leviticus, holiness touched objects and made them holy, and Haggai 2:13 shows defilement spreading more easily. In Jesus the holy one touches the unclean and holiness wins, the reversal the contagion laws of Leviticus 6 could not achieve.

'Let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. For our God is a consuming fire.' The altar fire of Leviticus 6 becomes a picture of God Himself, calling the church to the reverence the priests were taught to show.

study.oneStory:
In Eden God and humanity lived together without any need of an altar. After the fall the way back was guarded by cherubim and 'a whirling sword of flame,' Genesis 3:24. Fire marked the boundary between a holy God and sinful people. Leviticus 6 takes up that fire and gives it a new role: kept burning on the altar in the middle of the camp, it becomes the place where sinners are received rather than repelled.

It answers a question raised by chapters 1 to 5. If Israel's approach to God depends on offerings, who keeps the means of approach ready? The answer is a priesthood that never rests. The fire never goes out, the ashes are carried away, the grain offering rises morning and evening. The chapter shows the cost of maintaining fellowship with a holy God in a fallen world: it is endless.

It sets up the tension the rest of the story resolves. The priests grow careless: Eli's sons treat the offerings with contempt, 1 Samuel 2:17, and in Malachi's day the priests kindle 'useless fires,' Malachi 1:10. The fire can be kept, but it cannot change the people who keep it. The system itself, in its endless repetition, declares that it has not yet finished its work.

The story finds its answer in Christ. He is the priest who sits down because His sacrifice is complete, Hebrews 10:12, who bears sin in His body, 1 Peter 2:24, and whose holiness heals what it touches. At Pentecost the fire of God comes to rest on a people rather than an altar, Acts 2:3, and they become a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices, 1 Peter 2:5, and their bodies as living sacrifices, Romans 12:1.

The story ends in a city with no temple and no altar, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. No fire will need tending, because the presence it guarded will be everywhere. The priests who once served a hearth by night will be joined by all God's people who 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and the holiness that once broke clay pots will fill a renewed creation without destroying it.

quiz.q: What must never happen to the fire on the altar, according to this chapter?

options.text: It must be kept burning continually and never extinguished.
options.note: Verses 9, 12, and 13 all repeat this requirement for a perpetual, unceasing fire.

options.text: It must be put out every evening and relit each morning.
options.note: The text explicitly requires the opposite, a fire that continues burning without interruption.

options.text: It must be relit once a year at Passover.
options.note: The instruction concerns a continual fire, not an annual relighting ritual.

options.text: No instructions are given about the fire.
options.note: Verses 9 to 13 give detailed instructions specifically about maintaining the fire.

quiz.q: Where must Aaron and his sons eat the remainder of the grain offering?

options.text: In a holy place, the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.
options.note: Verse 16 specifies this exact location for eating the grain offering.

options.text: In their own homes, wherever they lived.
options.note: The text requires it be eaten in a holy place, not in ordinary homes.

options.text: Anywhere in the wilderness camp.
options.note: The requirement is specifically the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, a holy place, not anywhere in the camp.

options.text: No location is specified.
options.note: Verse 16 explicitly specifies the location.

quiz.q: What must be done with a clay pot in which the sin offering has been boiled?

options.text: It must be broken.
options.note: Verse 28 explicitly requires breaking the clay pot, while a bronze pot need only be scoured and rinsed.

options.text: It must be kept permanently in the sanctuary.
options.note: The text requires the pot be broken, not preserved.

options.text: It must be given to the worshiper who brought the offering.
options.note: The pot's disposal is prescribed as broken; it is not given away to the worshiper.

options.text: Nothing needs to be done with it.
options.note: Verse 28 gives a specific requirement for the clay pot.

quiz.q: What special grain offering must Aaron present on the day of his anointing, and every day after as the ongoing priestly portion?

options.text: A tenth of an ephah of fine flour, half offered in the morning and half in the evening, burned completely.
options.note: Verses 20 to 23 describe this offering and specify it must be burned completely, unlike ordinary grain offerings that priests eat.

options.text: A whole bull, burned entirely each morning.
options.note: The offering specified is a grain offering of fine flour, not a bull.

options.text: Nothing additional beyond the regular grain offering.
options.note: Verses 19 to 23 describe a specific, additional offering unique to the anointed priest.

options.text: No such offering is described.
options.note: Verses 19 to 23 give a detailed description of this offering.

quiz.q: When must a sin offering be burned rather than eaten by the priests, according to verse 30?

options.text: When its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place.
options.note: Verse 30 gives this exact condition, matching the procedure described earlier in chapter 4 for the priest's and congregation's sin offerings.

options.text: Whenever the offering is brought by a leader rather than a common person.
options.note: The distinguishing factor named in verse 30 is whether the blood entered the Tent of Meeting, not the rank of the one who sinned.

options.text: Only on the Sabbath day.
options.note: No such Sabbath restriction is mentioned in this verse.

options.text: No exception to eating the sin offering is given.
options.note: Verse 30 explicitly states this exception.

questions: The altar fire had to be tended continually, never allowed to go out. What spiritual disciplines in your own life need that same kind of continual, faithful tending rather than occasional attention?

The priests had to change clothes before carrying out the ashes, treating even that task with careful reverence. Where in your own service to God have you become careless about details that actually matter?

The most holy portions could only be eaten in a designated holy place, never casually. Do you treat your access to God, through prayer and His word, with the seriousness it deserves, or has it become routine?

The priest who ate the sin offering bore the weight of the people's guilt in that act. How does it change your view of Christ to know He literally bore your sin in His own body, not just symbolically?

Christ's sacrifice was offered once, and He sat down, His work finished, unlike the priests who stood daily repeating the ritual. Are you still striving to earn what Christ has already completed for you?

translationNotes.note: The fire must be kept burning, using the Hebrew tamid, continually, is the same word used elsewhere for the daily, regular offerings, tying together the ideas of unceasing fire and unceasing worship.

Anything that touches them will become holy describes a principle of contagious holiness in this ritual system, where contact with what is most holy conveys a derived sanctity requiring careful handling.

The distinction between breaking a clay pot and scouring a bronze one reflects the different porosity of the materials; clay could retain residue from the most holy offering in a way bronze would not.
